The operational guide was developed under the leadership of Dr. Knut Lönnroth (Global TB Programme, WHO, Switzerland), who wrote the first draft with assistance from Ms. Cecily Miller (American Thoracic Society, United States). Several experts reviewed and edited drafts, including Dr. Frank Bonsu (Ghana), Dr. Erwin Cooreman (WHO Myanmar), Dr. Jacob Creswell (Stop TB Partnership, Switzerland), Dr. Michel Gasana (Rwanda), Dr. Pedro Guillermo Suarez (United States), Dr. Irwin Law (WHO Switzerland), Dr. Ellen Mitchell (Netherlands), Dr. Lindiwe Mvusi (South Africa), Dr. Nobuyuki Nishikiori (WHO Western Pacific), Dr. Mao Tan Eang (Cambodia), Dr. Anja van ’t Hoog (Netherlands), Ms. Diana Weil (WHO Switzerland), Dr. Rajendra Yadav (WHO Cambodia), and Ms. Ruan Yunzhu (China). The online tool was developed by Dr. Nobuyuki Nishikiori, Dr. Knut Lönnroth, and Ms. Cecily Miller, with Dr. Anja van ’t Hoog assisting in the development of models for yield and cost of screening and diagnostic algorithms. The document was discussed in an expert consultation and a scientific symposium at the 45th Union World Conference on Lung Health in Barcelona, Spain, in 2014. Partial support for this product came from the United States Agency for International Development (USAID) under the TB CARE I Collaborative Agreement. The contents do not necessarily reflect the views of USAID or the United States Government. Active tuberculosis (TB) refers to disease caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis in individuals with signs or symptoms of active disease, distinguishing it from latent TB infection, which occurs without such signs or symptoms. Active TB case-finding, synonymous with systematic screening for active TB, typically involves screening outside health facilities. The number needed to screen (NNS) refers to the number of individuals who must undergo screening to diagnose one person with active TB. Passive TB case-finding is a patient-initiated pathway involving recognition of symptoms, access to care, presentation at a health facility, correct assessment by a health worker, and successful use of a diagnostic algorithm. Passive case-finding may include systematic screening if all individuals seeking care at a facility are systematically assessed for suspected TB. Risk groups are populations with significantly higher TB prevalence or incidence than the general population. Screening tests for active TB aim to distinguish individuals with a high likelihood of active TB from those unlikely to have it. Screening tests are not diagnostic; individuals with positive screening results require diagnostic evaluation. Second screening involves additional tests for individuals with positive initial screening results. Systematic screening for active TB involves identifying individuals with suspected TB in a predetermined target group using rapid tests or procedures, followed by diagnostic confirmation. More than one-third of the estimated 9 million people who develop TB annually are not diagnosed, notified, or started on treatment. Delays in treatment initiation due to various challenges result in poor health outcomes, catastrophic costs for families, and continued TB transmission. High-risk individuals and communities often have the least access to healthcare, exacerbating the disease's negative effects. These barriers, coupled with the global TB burden, necessitate intensified efforts for early identification and treatment of all TB cases. Systematic screening of high-risk groups is a key component of WHO's End TB Strategy (2016–2035). Systematic screening aims to ensure early detection and treatment, reduce poor treatment outcomes and adverse consequences, and decrease TB transmission to ultimately reduce future incidence. WHO guidelines provide principles and recommendations for prioritizing risk groups and selecting screening approaches. Screening should not be conducted indiscriminately on a mass scale due to high costs, low benefits, and potential for false positives. Screening must be targeted to high-risk groups and tailored to specific epidemiological, social, and health-system contexts. This document offers practical guidance for translating WHO's principles and recommendations into national or local screening strategies. It outlines six essential steps: assessing the situation, defining screening objectives, prioritizing risk groups, selecting screening tools and approaches, planning and budgeting for implementation, and monitoring and evaluating the strategy. These steps form an iterative cycle integrated with national TB and health system activities. Screening must be preceded by high-quality TB diagnosis, treatment, care, and support systems, with capacity to scale up as needed. A baseline analysis should demonstrate that the benefits of screening outweigh potential harms. Indiscriminate mass screening is expensive and has uncertain benefits, and screening low-risk groups may cause more harm than good. Prioritizing high-risk groups and selecting appropriate screening and diagnostic tests for each group and situation are essential.
